title:
Microplastics Are
Prevalent in Striped Bass and Shiner
Surfperch Tissues across San Francisco Bay, California

affiliation.name: San Francisco Estuary Institute , 4911 Central Ave , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The ingestion of microplastics by fish is widely documented, but the drivers of contamination and the movement of particles within organisms are still not well understood. We investigated microplastic contamination in sport fish caught from San Francisco Bay in California, USA. We compared microplastic contamination in striped bass (Morone saxatilis) and shiner surfperch (Cymatogaster aggregata). We observed an average of 5.9 ± 5.6 (Std Dev) microplastics per fish, with significantly higher overall contamination in striped bass but higher concentrations (microplastics/gram of tissue) in shiner surfperch. For each, we considered contamination relevant to their consumption by recreational anglers. For striped bass, where only the fillet is typically ingested, we found that contamination among tissues differed significantly (on average 3.8 ± 3.1 microplastics/fish fillets). Shiner surfperch, which are typically consumed whole, had an average body burden of 9.1 ± 1.2 microplastics/fish. Contamination varied significantly (p-value &lt; 0.0001) among sampling locations for shiner surfperch, with the highest amounts observed near urban centers (no significant spatial pattern was observed for striped bass). Our findings show microplastics in tissues beyond the gastrointestinal tract, posing concerns for fish health and suggesting that fish caught from San Francisco Bay are a pathway for human consumption of microplastics.</jats:p>

title:
Arsenate Adsorption
by Amorphous Titanium (Hydr)Oxides:
Governing Roles of Medium-Range Ordering and Surface Disorder
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Amorphous metal (hydr)oxides are used for oxyanion removal from water, yet the structural features responsible for their adsorption performance remain poorly understood. This paper systematically investigated how the ordering range and associated structural characteristics of amorphous titanium (hydr)oxides influence the adsorption of arsenate, used here as a model oxyanion. Six materials were synthesized with ordering ranges spanning approximately 4 to 43 Å. As the ordering range increased, a transition from microporous–mesoporous structures to predominantly mesoporous architectures was observed. Characterizations revealed progressive structural ordering with increasing synthesis aging temperature. The most amorphous sample exhibited stronger water binding, providing indirect evidence of fewer surrounding hydration clusters than in more ordered samples. However, despite possessing the highest specific surface area, the most amorphous material did not exhibit the highest arsenate uptake. Instead, the material aged at 140 °C achieved the greatest adsorption capacity, exceeding that of the fully amorphous material by &gt;20%. This adsorption maximum coincided with an intermediate ordering range, a transitional structural state, and a mesopore-dominated pore architecture. The results indicate that arsenate adsorption is not governed by surface area alone. Instead, the ordering range provides a useful descriptor linking atomic-scale structure, pore architecture, hydration behavior, and adsorption performance in amorphous metal (hydr)oxides.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Emerging contaminants (ECs) are increasingly detected in eutrophic lakes, yet their ecological contributions to phytoplankton community variation relative to conventional environmental factors remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the spatiotemporal occurrence of typical ECs and associated phytoplankton community variation in Taihu Lake, China. Phytoplankton abundance was significantly correlated with water temperature and total phosphorus (P &lt; 0.05). Among the EC groups, organochlorine pesticides (37.7%), per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (16.7%), and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (16.1%) showed strong associations with the spatiotemporal variation in phytoplankton community composition. Organochlorine pesticides explained 18.8% and 25.9% of the α-diversity variation in spring and summer, respectively, and interaction analyses suggested potential combined effects among contaminant groups. Water quality factors and ECs jointly explained 67.9% of the community variation, with stronger associations observed in summer than in spring. Higher dominance of Cryptomonas ovata in Gonghu Bay during spring and Microcystis sp. in Western Bay during summer was associated with reduced phytoplankton community diversity under combined gradients of eutrophication and ECs. These findings highlight the covariation of phytoplankton communities with eutrophication and ECs and provide new insights into ecological risk assessment and algal bloom management in shallow eutrophic lakes.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamic
Hydrogen-Bonded
Hydration Networks Mitigate
Organic–Inorganic Fouling in Nanofiltration

affiliation.name: University of Science and Technology of China , , ,
University of Science and Technology of China , , ,
University of Science and Technology of China , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydration layers are widely recognized as the molecular basis of antifouling membrane interfaces, yet their role is still largely viewed through a static barrier picture. The dynamic response of hydrated membrane–water interfaces to approaching foulants, particularly under organic–inorganic mixed fouling conditions, remains poorly understood. Here, using poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (pSBMA)-modified nanofiltration membranes as a model zwitterionic interface, we reveal that fouling reversibility is strongly influenced by the dynamic stability of hydrogen-bonded hydration networks at the membrane–water interface. Molecular simulations combined with sum-frequency generation spectroscopy demonstrate that pSBMA sustains a strongly hydrogen-bonded interfacial water structure with preferential water dipole orientation under silicate and alginate perturbation, thereby suppressing long-lived foulant residence near the membrane surface. Real-time surface plasmon resonance measurements further confirm weakened irreversible foulant anchoring and enhanced interfacial reversibility. As a result, pSBMA-modified nanofiltration membranes reduced flux decline during mixed-foulant filtration to ∼6% and achieved &gt;91% flux recovery after physical cleaning, accompanied by lower organic and inorganic foulant residuals. Repeated filtration–cleaning tests with real secondary effluent further confirmed nearly complete flux recovery in complex water matrices. These findings revisit zwitterionic antifouling by shifting the focus from static surface hydration to the dynamic stability of hydrogen-bonded hydration networks, providing a mechanistic basis for understanding and regulating fouling reversibility.</jats:p>

title:
Mechanistic Understanding
of Breath-Borne Bacterial
Inactivation Kinetics in Oxidant-Rich and Natural Air
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bioaerosols play a central role in respiratory infection transmission, but how atmospheric oxidants affect their viability, especially in human respiratory fluids, remains unexplored. Here, we investigated the inactivation of five bacterial species with distinct cell envelope architectures (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Mycobacterium smegmatis) suspended in human exhaled breath condensate (EBC) droplets exposed to gas-phase hydroxyl radicals (•OH) produced by ultraviolet irradiation of H2O2. Compared with the other three exposure conditions, the •OH-generating (H2O2+UV) treatment caused the greatest viability loss, with 4-h survival ranging from 24.3% (E. coli) to 63.0% (M. smegmatis). Gram-negative bacteria were sensitive to both H2O2 and •OH, whereas Gram-positive species resisted H2O2 but were inactivated by •OH. M. smegmatis showed the highest tolerance. Inactivation accelerated in smaller droplets, and the size-dependent kinetics were characterized using Weibull and first-order models incorporating surface-area-to-volume ratio. Morphological, biochemical, and metabolomic analyses indicated that the observed inactivation differences were associated with bacterial envelope types and surface characteristics. •OH preferentially degrades outer membrane glycolipids in Gram-negative bacteria and oxidizes cytoplasmic membrane lipids in Gram-positive bacteria, while all species shared a core signature of nucleic acid oxidative damage. These findings provide a molecular understanding of bacterial inactivation kinetics in human EBC droplets and may inform the assessment of bioaerosol transmission risks.</jats:p>

over Transient Electrical Heating and Associated Benefits

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Soil serves as a significant sink for microplastics, posing considerable risks to both the ecological and human health. The diverse composition and dynamic transformation of microplastics present major challenges for remediation as conventional strategies often fail to achieve efficient and complete decomposition. In this study, biochar was applied to microplastic-contaminated soil as a conductive material to initiate transient electric heating under a low-power input. This approach facilitated near-complete decomposition of soil microplastics (&gt;95.0%) across the tested soil and microplastic types while preventing soil hardening. Specifically, electric heating enhanced interactions between soil microplastics and the biochar conductor, leading to the formation of highly aromatic carbon (HAC). The resulting HAC not only improved soil microecology but also supported the growth of pak choi (Brassica campestris L. ssp.). The newly formed HAC was found to upregulate the expression of auxin-responsive gene families, including Aux/IAA and GH3, in the roots. HAC enriched tryptamine in the rhizosphere, and tryptamine abundance was positively correlated with the relative abundance of Sphingomonas, a genus with a reported capacity to convert tryptamine-derived intermediates toward indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) biosynthesis. These findings demonstrate that transient electric heating offers a sustainable strategy for decomposing diverse soil microplastics and that the remediated soil remains safe and conducive for agricultural production.</jats:p>

title:
Unveiling Phase-Dependent
Fe–O Bond-Guided
Nitrate Reduction at Biocathodes: Balancing Interfacial Reactivity
and Iron Bioavailability

affiliation.name: Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Anaerobic Biotechnology , ,
Jiangsu Collaborative Innovation Center of Technology and Material of Water Treatment , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Iron oxides are widespread in anoxic water environments, yet how their structures regulate microbial nitrate reduction remains unclear. Here, we reveal that phase-dependent Fe–O bond characteristics guide denitrification in bioelectrochemical system (BES) by balancing lattice-iron bioavailability and interfacial electrochemical reactivity at biocathodes. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that surface Fe–O bond covalency was associated with the thermodynamic barrier to lattice-iron release. α-Fe2O3, with the most negative ICOHP, exhibited the strongest Fe–O bonding and restricted iron release, thereby limiting microbial iron acquisition and downstream Fe–S cluster assembly. In contrast, γ-Fe2O3 and γ-FeOOH exhibited higher surface electroactivity but suffered from structural instability, evidenced by phase transformation, cell encrustation, and elevated microbial mortality. With mixed valence and balanced Fe–O bonding characteristics, Fe3O4 achieved the highest denitrification efficiency (17.8-fold enhancement over its abiotic control), which enabled direct Fe(II) uptake via the FeoAB system, bypassing siderophore-dependent acquisition and simultaneously activating both TonB-mediated iron acquisition and Fur-flavin-regulated respiratory pathways. This dual-pathway activation supported enhancement in biomass growth, intracellular electron transfer, and Fe–S cluster-dependent enzymatic activity. These findings help establish Fe–O bond characteristics as a key structural factor for Fe–N coupling and offer a structural perspective for rational design of iron-oxide-based nitrate-removal technologies.</jats:p>

title:
A Perspective on
the Development of Novel In Situ
Remediation of Contaminated Sediments Using Black Carbon

affiliation.name: Norway and Norwegian University of Life Sciences (NMBU) , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The field of contaminated sediment remediation was disrupted two decades ago by the emergence of a new way to reduce risk in situ through the amendment of black carbon sorbents─activated carbon and specialized biochars. This required a paradigm shift from a focus on reducing pollutant mass to reducing exposure through bioavailability control. Sorbent amendment technology has advanced from laboratory and pilot field demonstrations to full-scale applications at many sites and has recently been incorporated in USEPA records of decision at Superfund sites. This perspective summarizes critical points in advancing the new technology: 1) accurate problem definition recognizing that sediment pollutant mass reduction does not necessarily lead to risk reduction, 2) breakthroughs in bioavailability science and unraveling the role of native black carbon in sediments, 3) demonstration of pollutant bioavailability reduction with strong sorption, 4) quantitative descriptions of the process, 5) addressing the challenges of mercury, 6) understanding unintended consequences, and 7) development of freely dissolved concentrations as a key bioavailability metric with regulatory and stakeholder engagement. The lessons learned in this journey from early science through technological maturity can help inform other technologies that are in development to address evolving threats to the environment.</jats:p>

title: Environmentally Persistent Free Radicals on Aged Polyamide Microplastics Drive Neurotoxicity in Eisenia fetida via a Glutamate-Centered Cascade
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrogen-containing microplastics (N-MPs) are widespread in soil and often exhibit distinct environmental behaviors and effects owing to their unique elemental composition and molecular structure. However, their toxicity to soil organisms remains poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, the toxicity of pristine and aged polyamides (PA) was evaluated in earthworms (Eisenia fetida), a representative soil invertebrate. At 0.01% (w/w), aged PA increased the magnitude of body-weight loss, MDA levels, and AChE activity by 24.4%, 11.6%, and 24.1%, respectively, relative to pristine PA-MPs. Greater accumulation of aged PA-MPs was accompanied by enhanced oxidative damage and neurotoxicity. Integrated multiomics, quantitative real-time PCR, and biomarker analyses revealed that oxidative stress-mediated membrane damage promoted glutamate accumulation, receptor overactivation, Ca2+ overload, synaptic injury, and ultimately neurotoxicity. Pharmacological interventions and transmission electron microscopy of the ventral nerve cord provided functional and morphological support for this cascade. Radical quenching and comparative leachate bioassays further supported the important contribution of environmentally persistent free radicals in aged PA-MPs to neuronal damage. These findings define a mechanistic pathway for aged microplastic-induced neurotoxicity and provide a basis for assessing the ecological risks of aged N-MPs in soils.</jats:p>

title:
Plant
Oxidative Stress Mediates the Synergistic Transformation
of Benzotriazole Ultraviolet Stabilizers in Rhizosphere Soil: Insights
from Dual Exposure Pathways

affiliation.name: Chinese Research Academy of Environment Sciences , , ,
Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Benzotriazole ultraviolet stabilizers (BUVs) are widespread emerging contaminants in soil. However, their transformation in the rhizosphere and the regulatory effects of plant oxidative stress on rhizosphere remediation remain unclear. The objective of this study was to investigate these effects using molecular simulations and rhizosphere and foliar exposure experiments. The removal efficiency of the four BUVs was 15–46% higher in the rhizosphere of Helianthus annuus than under natural soil degradation. The plant rhizosphere promoted BUV desorption from soil and induced hydroxylation as a specific transformation pathway. Direct rhizosphere exposure triggered oxidative stress and accelerated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation in soil. Rhizosphere ROS contributed approximately 31.2%–42.7% to BUV transformation. Foliar exposure experiments suggested that plant oxidative stress is an important contributor to rhizosphere ROS generation. Under BUV stress, plant oxidative stress regulated the composition of dissolved organic matter (DOM) and the selective enrichment of bacteria, including Acidobacteriota, Actinomycota, and Bacteroidota. Multivariate correlation network analysis suggested that foliar exposure resulted in more complex interactions among rhizosphere microenvironmental characteristics than did direct rhizosphere exposure. This study provides insights into BUV transformation in the rhizosphere and establishes a framework for plant signal-guided rhizosphere remediation strategies.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Racial disparities in the incidence of, and mortality from, aggressive breast cancers are a pressing public health issue. Many factors have been investigated in these inequities; however, the role of toxicant exposures is not well characterized. We and others have identified substantial inequities in chemical biomarker concentrations by race. The goal of this study was to test the hypothesis that exposure to these chemicals is linked to biological changes relevant to aggressive breast cancers, such as dysregulation of the Hallmarks of Cancer. We used high-throughput transcriptomic profiling of normal primary human breast epithelial cells from diverse donors (n = 6) to test the effects of 8 chemicals (cadmium, lead, arsenic, copper, PFNA, BPA, BPS, and p,p’-DDE) with documented exposure disparities by race/ethnicity across 3 concentrations (100 nM, 1 μM, and 10 μM). Across chemicals, we identified that pathways related to cell cycle regulation and protein secretion were commonly affected. Through bioinformatic estimation of cell-type proportions, we found that metals like lead and cadmium induced cell-type shifts, consistent with the dysregulated cellular plasticity cancer hallmark. Lead- and arsenic-response genes were enriched for genes associated with poor breast cancer survival in the Cancer Genome Atlas. Integrating concentration–response modeling and chemical biomonitoring data, BPA, p,p’-DDE, copper, and lead elicited expression changes at concentrations relevant to the US population. Finally, we identified substantial interindividual heterogeneity in response to chemical classes, with heavy metals producing the largest dose-responsive transcriptional effects. These findings highlight the value of high-throughput transcriptomics as a new approach methodology (NAM) in quantifying how common exposures may impact aggressive breast cancer-associated biological processes.</jats:p>

title:
From
Molecular Topography
to Ozone Pollution: Species
Sources and Photochemical Kinetics of Individual Organic Peroxyl Radicals

affiliation.name: Shenyang Ecological Environment Monitoring Center of Liaoning Province , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ground-level ozone (O3) poses significant threats to global public health and climate change. Organic peroxyl radicals (RO2) serve as crucial intermediates in atmospheric O3 formation. Although individual RO2 species exhibit distinct reactivities, the quantification and source attribution of individual RO2 species remain poorly understood. Here, we address the challenge by integrating high-resolution field observations with fundamental theoretical kinetics within a novel hybrid receptor-kinetic modeling framework. The concentration and composition of RO2 species exhibit significant seasonal and diurnal dependencies. In summer, the 19 RO2 pool was characterized by a substantial contribution from biogenic sources (29%), particularly isoprene-derived species (ISOPOBO2). Conversely, the wintertime RO2 composition shifts, dramatically dominated by industrial emissions (41%), notably ethylene-derived species (HOCH2CH2O2). Source apportionment via the RO2+NO pathway further demonstrates that O3 photochemical formation potentials align closely with the kinetics of RO2 production. A data-driven machine learning model effectively captures the contribution of individual RO2 species to O3 formation in summer, but it shows significant deviations from kinetic simulations in winter. The framework establishes a dynamic framework to support daytime O3 mitigation by quantifying the high-time-resolution RO2 radical pool from field VOCs measurements.</jats:p>

title:
Relative Humidity
Modulates Nitration and Ring Fragmentation
during Heterogeneous Oxidation of Catechol by Nitrate Radicals
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Catechol is an important biomass-burning-derived phenolic compound and a precursor to secondary organic aerosols (SOAs). Although nitrate radicals (NO3) are recognized as major nighttime oxidants, the influence of the aerosol water content on heterogeneous NO3 oxidation of phenolic compounds remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of relative humidity (RH = 0–90%) on the heterogeneous oxidation of catechol thin films by nitrate radicals generated from the reaction of O3 and NO2. Product formation was characterized using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, UV–visible spectroscopy, electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS), ultrahigh-pressure liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UHPLC–MS), and ion chromatography–mass spectrometry (IC–MS). Under dry conditions, oxidation favored nitration and oligomerization pathways, producing mono-, di-, and trinitrocatechols together with catechol dimers and trimers. These products exhibited enhanced absorption in the 300–500 nm region, characteristic of brown carbon chromophores. Increasing RH progressively suppressed the relative nitration capacity of the NO3/N2O5 system while promoting oxidative ring-opening reactions, leading to the formation of dicarboxylic acids, including cis,cis-muconic acid, 2,3-dihydroxymaleic acid, and oxalic acid. Product distributions revealed a transition from functionalization-dominated chemistry at low RH to fragmentation-dominated chemistry at high RH. These results indicate that RH strongly controls nighttime nitrate radical oxidation of biomass-burning phenolics by shifting product formation from light-absorbing nitroaromatic brown carbon toward highly oxygenated fragmentation products. The findings provide new mechanistic insights into the role of aerosol water in governing the chemical aging and optical evolution of biomass-burning aerosols.</jats:p>

title:
Electrification,
Lightweighting, and Materials Supply:
A Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment of the U.S. Light-Duty Vehicle Fleet

affiliation.name: The University of New South Wales , , , ,
The University of New South Wales , , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrification and lightweighting are reshaping vehicle designs and materials demand, with uncertain net effects on life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Most existing fleet studies treat material choices, materials markets, and vehicle adoption separately, without capturing feedbacks between design, supply chains, and consumer behavior. This study develops an integrated system dynamics–life cycle assessment (SD–LCA) framework to explore these interactions for the U.S. light-duty vehicle fleet from 2000 to 2060. The model extends an established powertrain diffusion framework by endogenizing vehicle body material selection, battery capacity evolution, and materials market responses, linking these dynamics to a bottom-up life cycle assessment of fleet GHG emissions. Scenario analysis shows that increasing aluminum use in lightweight gasoline vehicles improves their utility and market share, largely offsetting use-phase GHG savings and yielding only modest reductions in total fleet emissions. In contrast, faster battery electric vehicle adoption raises cradle-to-gate emissions but more than compensates through lower use-phase emissions, reducing total fleet GHGs. Shifts in vehicle material demand also generate transient imbalances in steel and aluminum markets, temporarily lowering recycled fraction and increasing cradle-to-gate emissions. The SD–LCA framework demonstrates how feedbacks between vehicle design, materials supply, and consumer adoption shape fleet decarbonization pathways.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Exposure to trihalomethanes (THMs) has been linked to reduced human semen quality, but the critical windows of vulnerability and underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We therefore measured untargeted seminal plasma metabolomics to identify metabolic biomarkers and biological pathways linking blood THM concentrations to repeated measurements of semen quality (4146 measurements over a 3 month follow-up period) among 762 healthy Chinese men. We found inverse associations between blood THM concentrations (i.e., chloroform, bromodichloromethane, and chlorinated THMs) and semen volume and total sperm count (all P values &lt;0.05), which were most pronounced for exposure measured 70–90 days prior to semen collection (corresponding to the early stage of spermatogenesis). Metabolome-wide association analyses identified 90 metabolites that were simultaneously associated with blood THM concentrations and sperm-quality parameters. Mediation analyses further revealed that 44 metabolites, enriched in the pathways of unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, linoleic acid metabolism, pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis, and β-alanine metabolism, mediated a considerable proportion (8.1–41.3%) of the inverse relationships between THM exposure and semen quality. Our results suggest that THM exposure during the early stage of spermatogenesis is associated with reduced human semen quality, potentially driven by perturbations in lipid metabolism, steroid hormone synthesis, and antioxidant-related metabolisms.</jats:p>

title:
Winter and Summer
Differences in Oxylipin Responses
to Ambient Particles: Roles of Sizes and Constituents

affiliation.name: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College , , ,

Capital Medical University, Beijing Institute of Heart, Lung and Blood Vessel Diseases , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) has been associated with increased mortality risk, but whether it is more harmful on colder or warmer days is unclear. Here, we investigate seasonal variations in PM2.5 mass, sizes, constituents, and their association with oxylipin changes in humans. In a panel study of 123 adults in Beijing, we measured 27 PM2.5 metrics and five circulating lipoxygenase-derived oxylipins (i.e., leukotriene B4 [LTB4], 5-, 8-, 12-, and 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid [HETE]) across winter and summer. PM2.5 exposure was associated with peak oxylipin increases at lag 0–1 days. Across particle size fractions and constituents, oxylipin increases ranged from 3.3% to 114.2%, with the most robust associations for ultrafine particles, accumulation mode particles, organic carbon, and chloride. Furthermore, an exposure-response relationship between UFP and oxylipins was observed only in summer. An IQR increase in UFP was associated with oxylipin changes of 12.9–97.7% in summer and −7.7 to 18.8% in winter. Conversely, oxylipin increases associated with accumulation mode particles and organic carbon were greater in winter. These findings suggest that the sizes and constituents of PM2.5 may partially explain the seasonal difference in the health effect of PM2.5 exposure, helping identify components associated with stronger biomarker responses in specific seasons.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Restoring soil biota and dissolved organic matter (DOM) is essential for sustainable ecological restoration of coal mine sites. Protists, as key microbial predators, are recognized as regulators of multiple belowground processes, yet their roles in shaping DOM during ecological restoration remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a field-scale coal mine ecological restoration chronosequence using vegetation surveys, ultrahigh-resolution Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS), and high-throughput Illumina sequencing. Restoration increased plant diversity, coverage, and aboveground biomass, which are key resources for soil organic matter inputs. Soil DOM shifted toward more thermodynamically stable compounds, with enhanced chemodiversity during the restoration process. Protistan diversity, particularly of phagotrophic taxa, increased with restoration age, potentially exerting top-down control that increased bacterial diversity but suppressed fungal diversity. Co-occurrence network analysis and random forest modeling revealed that plant biomass was positively linked with phagotrophic diversity, which might influence DOM composition through direct transformation of organic matter (OM) or indirect regulation of bacterial transformation of OM, contributing to the accumulation of recalcitrant molecules with high stability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized trophic cascade linking protists to DOM chemodiversity at the molecular level, highlighting the importance of integrating protistan regulation into soil ecological restoration strategies for mine sites.</jats:p>

title: Heavy-Duty Diesel Vehicle Deterioration: Impact of Vehicle Age and Emission Control Technology on NO x Emissions
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study examines the effect of aging and deterioration on NOx emissions from heavy-duty diesel trucks (HDDTs) with different emission control technologies, including Engine Control only, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). In-use tailpipe emissions were measured from 12,023 HDDTs from 13 roadside measurement campaigns conducted in California and Utah between 2008 and 2024. Vehicle registration records and the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) engine certification database were used to identify engine NOx control technology. At younger ages, SCR-equipped HDDTs generally emitted significantly less NOx than non-SCR-equipped HDDTs. However, after several years of aging, NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs were comparable to or exceeded those from non-SCR-equipped HDDTs across locations, engine manufacturers, and engine model years. Although cumulative lifetime emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs remained lower than non-SCR HDDTs, the reduction in lifetime NOx emissions was substantially smaller than estimated by EPA’s MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES). MOVES predicts an 80% reduction in lifetime NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs, whereas our estimate is approximately 32%. These findings may indicate that the long-term benefits of SCR for reducing HDDT NOx emissions are smaller than expected and highlight the need for continued emissions monitoring of in-use HDDTs.</jats:p>

title:
Chasing Bubbles:
Toward a Standardized Approach for
Quantifying Methane Ebullition Using Bubble Traps in Streams and Rivers

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ebullition transports large quantities of the potent greenhouse gas methane (CH4) from stream sediments into the atmosphere. However, the use of different sampling designs complicates comparisons of CH4 emissions estimates between studies. Here, we present the first systematic review of sampling designs used in the past for assessing fluvial CH4 ebullition rates. In addition, we conducted field experiments to estimate the optimal number of bubble traps and the length of the sampling period, and to assess uncertainties in determining CH4 content in the emitted bubbles. Our results demonstrate considerable spatial variability in bubble fluxes (0–4.8 L m–2 d–1) and CH4 content in the bubbles (0.01–67%), necessitating a larger number of bubble traps than typically deployed in streams. Using fewer traps leads to greater deviations in CH4 ebullition estimates than shorter deployment times. Therefore, the robust sampling design should account for strong small-scale heterogeneity in streams through an adequate number of bubble traps and link bubble fluxes to trap-specific gas content. It should also consider the risk of CH4 concentration decreases in accumulated bubbles over a few days, primarily due to redissolution, followed by oxidation and leakage.</jats:p>

title:
Post-Regulation
of Nitrogen Configurations in Nitrogen-Doped
Carbon Electrodes for Enhanced Capacitive Deionization

affiliation.name: Shanghai Institute of Pollution Control and Ecological Security , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrogen doping is widely used to enhance the electrochemical performance of carbon materials, yet its effectiveness is often limited by electrochemically inactive or inaccessible nitrogen configurations. Here, we develop a coupling-agent-mediated amidation strategy to postregulate nitrogen-doped carbon, selectively enriching amino nitrogen while tailoring the distribution of pyridinic, pyrrolic, and graphitic nitrogen. The introduced −NH2 groups elevate the surface charge density, which is favorable for ion adsorption and diffusion. Density functional theory calculations, together with electrochemical kinetic analyses, reveal that edge-type nitrogen, particularly the lone electron pairs on amino nitrogen, can strongly interact with salt ions, resulting in effective electrical-double-layer compression and shortened ion diffusion distance. Consequently, the optimized electrode achieves a specific adsorption capacity of 70.3 mgNaCl g–1 and a time-averaged adsorption rate of 2.3 mgNaCl g–1 min–1 in 1000 mg L–1 NaCl solution at a cell voltage of 1.6 V. Its electrosorption behavior toward monovalent and divalent cations is also systematically evaluated in synthetic brines and actual industrial recirculating cooling water. This study provides a facile, powerful strategy to rationally design carbon electrodes for high-performance electrochemical ion storage and separation applications.</jats:p>

title:
River
Plastic Retention and Export across Europe

affiliation.name: University Marine Research Institute INMAR, University of Cádiz and European University of the Seas , , , ,
University Marine Research Institute INMAR, University of Cádiz and European University of the Seas , , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Rivers play a central role in the global distribution of plastic pollution. Despite recent research showing that the majority of plastic is not transported to the sea, most plastic transport models have not explicitly included plastic retention in rivers. We propose a new model to quantify micro- and macroplastic retention on land and in rivers, and export toward the sea. Of the 3.55 Mt year–1 of plastics emitted to the environment, only 0.1% of microplastics and 0.5% of macroplastics are exported from the river outlet. This results in 16.8 (15.7–35.1) kt year–1 of microplastic and 3.2 (1.4–12.1) kt year–1 macroplastic export. Rivers store plastic, retaining 68.3 (156.5–350.1) kt year–1 of microplastics (5.3%) and 84.6 (37.2–320.5) kt year–1 of macroplastics (2.5%), while the greatest proportion of plastic remains on land. Although large basin size and high plastic emission to land characterize high absolute micro- and macroplastic retention and export, large basin size is a weaker predictor for high plastic retention and export per capita. By aggregating ranks for plastic export and retention, we provide a new and comprehensive outlook on the most polluting rivers of Europe. This work provides crucial baseline estimates for plastic pollution in light of missing plastic reduction quotas to guide future prioritization and assessment of mitigation actions.</jats:p>

title:
Phage-Based Biofilm
Control in Engineered Water Environments

affiliation.name: Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology (Eawag) , , ,
The George Washington University , , , ,
place: Washington, District of Columbia, United States, 20052

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.</jats:p>

title:
Monitoring Advanced
Hydration Station (AHS) Water
Quality in Flint, MI, School Buildings: Field Grab Sampling and Filter-Based
Lead Assessment
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>School drinking water lead exposure remains a public health concern. In addition, time-variant lead concentrations pose challenges to monitoring practices. This study evaluates the lead (and, for some experiments, bacterial) removal performance of advanced hydration stations (AHS) with membrane filters, activated carbon block filters, and LED UV disinfection in Flint, Michigan. Laboratory challenge testing and more than 400 grab samples were collected from influent and effluent water from over 70 field-deployed AHS units during three sampling campaigns in 2022 and 2023. Our study confirmed that AHS units effectively removed lead. The median influent lead concentrations ranged from 6 to 14 μg/L, with 53% of samples exceeding 10 μg/L. Lead levels in effluent water were almost all below the detection limit (98% of samples). Effluent bacteria concentrations monitored during the first field sampling campaign in 2022 were all below detection, and removal during challenge testing were &gt;2.6 log reduction. A subset of filters (n = 21) from those harvested in July 2022 were acid-extracted to assess the total accumulation of lead. This information, along with the cumulative volume of water processed, was used to calculate a volume-averaged lead concentration that represents avoided lead exposure and identifies potential hot spots of lead release to prioritize remediation activities. The outcomes of this monitoring campaign demonstrate the effectiveness of the AHS units at removing lead and bacteria, and the importance of using filter-based monitoring to inform AHS maintenance and identify upstream sources of lead.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Material recovery and circularity analysis offers critical insights for understanding future scenarios and informing strategic decisions toward resource use. However, existing approaches often lack the granularity and breadth needed to capture supply chain dynamics and economy-wide impacts simultaneously. We introduce a novel quantitative framework─Supply Chain Operations Research through Physical Input-Output (SCORPIO)─that addresses this gap by enabling multi-scale assessment of material recovery strategies across both supply chain and macroeconomic levels. To demonstrate SCORPIO’s capabilities, we apply it to flat glass flows in the United States, examining waste valorization practices, including open- and closed-loop recycling. By assessing economic, workforce, and environmental indicators, SCORPIO reveals the potential outcomes and trade-offs of different waste valorization solutions in a holistic manner. Results show that both open-loop and closed-loop recycling of glass from utility solar and commercial buildings have the potential for positive economic impacts at the supply chain and economy level. However, the effect on environmental impacts was less certain, with open-loop recycling generally performing better than closed-loop pathways. This case study illustrates how the SCORPIO framework can support stakeholders navigating the transition toward increased material recovery, offering a methodological foundation applicable to other material systems facing environmental and resource challenges.</jats:p>

title:
Convergent Biogenic
Magnetite Formation from Diverse
Iron (Oxyhydr)oxide Precursors Drives Cr(VI) Reduction via an Environmental
Battery Mechanism

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Iron (oxyhydr)oxides mediate electron flux across coupled biogeochemical cycles in anoxic environments, yet whether their biogenic transformation feeds back to reshape interfacial electron transfer efficiency remains unresolved. Here, five structurally distinct iron (oxyhydr)oxide precursors (ferrihydrite, goethite, magnetite, wüstite, and hematite) were exposed to anaerobic sulfur-oxidizing bioreactors under Cr(VI) stress, and their transformation trajectories were tracked using synchrotron EXAFS spectroscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, DFT calculations, and metagenomic profiling. Mineral bioavailability decreased in the order ferrihydrite &gt; goethite &gt; magnetite &gt; wüstite &gt; hematite, a hierarchy governed by lattice iron-leaching energetics quantified via DFT (Efev from −8.96 eV for ferrihydrite to 5.76 eV for hematite). Despite this wide disparity in precursor lability, all biotransformation trajectories converged on magnetite as the thermodynamically stable end point. In the ferrihydrite system, biogenic magnetite reached 60% of the final solid phase and operated as an in situ “environmental battery” (storing and releasing electrons through reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) lattice cycling), lowering interfacial charge transfer resistance and producing a 4.77-fold higher pseudo-first-order Cr(VI) reduction rate constant than the mineral-free biotic control (C-S). Metagenomic analysis revealed mineral-specific restructuring of the microbial community toward a tightly coupled sulfur–iron redox network. These results reframe precursor mineralogy from a determinant of intrinsic reactivity to a kinetic regulator of biogenic electron-buffer formation, providing a mechanistic basis for mineral-informed bioremediation design.</jats:p>

title:
From
Bench-Scale Experiments to Technical Scale-Up:
Rethinking Sorption Research for the Removal of Trace Organic Contaminants
from Water

affiliation.name: North Carolina State University , , 915 Partners Way , , ,
The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station , , 123 Huntington Street , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater systems are increasingly challenged by trace organic contaminants (TrOCs), including PFAS, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and other persistent and highly mobile contaminants that occur at ultralow concentrations in complex water matrices. Sorption-based treatment processes remain central to TrOC removal because they can concentrate dilute contaminants without generating potentially toxic transformation products. However, much of the current sorption literature remains disconnected from the needs of performance prediction and technical scale-up. Equilibrium and kinetic parameters are often derived under simplified laboratory conditions, using empirically fitted models, elevated contaminant concentrations, and/or nonrepresentative water matrices, limiting their physical interpretability and transferability across treatment scenarios. This review critically examines three interconnected areas governing the engineering relevance of sorption data: thermodynamic principles governing sorption equilibria, mechanistic interpretation of sorption kinetics, and the evaluation and transition of novel sorbents to scaled treatment systems. By identifying limitations in prevailing experimental practices and aligning equilibrium characterization, kinetic modeling, and sorbent evaluation with application-relevant conditions, this review provides a framework for generating mechanistically grounded sorption data to support material selection and translate laboratory-derived sorption data into process design parameters for pilot- and full-scale TrOC treatment systems.</jats:p>

title: No Significant Elimination of Perfluoroctanesulfonate and Other Common Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances by Adult Fathead Minnows, Pimephales promelas
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bioaccumulation dynamics of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) remain poorly understood, and kinetic-based information is lacking across environmental gradients, particularly for Cyprinidae, the largest and most diverse fish family. We examined the influences of pH (6.5, 7.5) and salinity (0.3 g/L, 3.0 g/L) on uptake and elimination kinetics of 19 PFAS, which were selected at low concentrations not eliciting standardized adverse outcomes, in the common Cyprinidae, Pimephales promelas. These PFAS consisted of short- and long-chain perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonates (PFSAs), a sulfonamide, and fluorotelomer sulfonates. Water, whole-body tissue, and plasma were collected over time, and samples were analyzed via liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Rapid uptake was observed in tissue, reaching pseudo-steady-state conditions within 24–96 h of exposure initiation; uptake rates increased with chain length but were not influenced (p &gt; 0.05) by pH or salinity. During four separate experiments, no significant (p &gt; 0.05) elimination was observed for PFDA, PFDoDA, PFTeDA, total PFOS, PFOSA, and 8:2 FTSA. Kinetic-based bioaccumulation factors (BAFs) increased with chain length for PFCAs and PFSAs, and exceedances of BAF cutoff values were identified. No significant (p &gt; 0.05) elimination of these PFAS indicates that Cyprinidae should be considered during future bioaccumulation studies.</jats:p>

title:
Economic Potential
of Nuclear Power in the Transportation
Sector: Analysis of E-Fuels as An Alternative Fuel for Total
Cost of Ownership and Vehicle Emissions

affiliation.name: U.S. Department of Energy , , , ,
place: Washington, District of Columbia, United States, 20585

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Advanced nuclear reactors could expand U.S. nuclear energy beyond electricity generation into transportation by supplying heat and power for hydrogen and synthetic hydrocarbon fuel production. We evaluated nuclear-enabled hydrogen for fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and nuclear-derived electro-fuels (e-fuels) for internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) and hybrid vehicles across selected light-, medium-, and heavy-duty classes. Economic performance was assessed using total cost of ownership (TCO), and environmental performance was evaluated using life-cycle emissions. We then estimated carbon abatement costs for alternative fuel/vehicle pathways relative to conventional gasoline and diesel systems. Our findings indicate that conventional ICEVs fueled by gasoline or diesel generally remain the lowest-cost options in 2035. For small sport utility vehicles (SUVs), however, hybrid vehicles using nuclear-based e-fuels and battery electric vehicles (BEVs) with home charging increase TCO modestly relative to gasoline vehicles, while e-fuels achieve the lowest emissions among the alternatives. In long-haul trucking, hydrogen and e-fuels show potential, with marginal TCO increases relative to conventional systems and relatively low abatement costs. Although hydrogen and e-fuels produced with advanced nuclear reactors remain relatively expensive, continued advances in reactors, electrolysis, and fuel synthesis, together with scale economies, could improve competitiveness, diversify transportation fuel options, and reduce emissions.</jats:p>

title:
Evaluating
Emergency
Emission Controls During an Unprecedented
Regional Haze Event Using Causal Machine Learning

affiliation.name: Tianjin Key Laboratory of Software Experience and Human Computer Interaction , ,
Beijing Municipal Pollution Source Management Center , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Emergency emission controls are widely implemented to mitigate severe haze, yet their effectiveness is difficult to disentangle from meteorological variability and concurrent changes in activities. Here, we develop a three-step evaluation approach integrating air quality meteorological normalization, augmented synthetic control, and machine-learning prediction to causally quantify intervention-attributable changes in local emission strength and ambient pollutant concentrations. Applied to Shijiazhuang’s unprecedented 45-day “Sharp Sword to Cut Haze” campaign in 2016, the approach revealed that local emission strengths of PM2.5, PM10, SO2, NO2, and CO were reduced by 4.3%, 4.8%, 15.8%, 5.8%, and 15.3%, respectively. Corresponding concentrations fell by 42.1 (14.8%), 47.4 (12.4%), 13.8 (16.6%), 15.8 (15.5%) μg·m–3, and 0.9 mg·m–3 (19.6%). Observation-based PM2.5 source apportionment results independently supported these estimates: contributions from vehicle emissions, steelmaking, and coal combustion were 4.1%, 11.0%, and 21.7% lower, respectively, than during the corresponding period in 2017. Despite stringent controls, PM2.5 averaged 243.2 μg·m–3 during the intervention period. Thus, stringent local controls substantially reduced emissions, but regional transport and unfavorable meteorology partly offset the resulting air quality benefits, highlighting the need for coordinated regional mitigation.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The formation of polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) in industrial thermal processes is traditionally attributed to solid carbon precursors via de novo synthesis. Carbon monoxide (CO), despite serving as an operational indicator of incomplete combustion, has not been directly implicated as a molecular carbon source for dioxin generation. Here, we provide definitive experimental and mechanistic evidence that CO can be catalytically converted into dioxins and dioxin-like compounds through a sequential reaction network mediated by fly ash. Using fixed-bed reactors packed with real fly ash, we isolate CO, H2O, and HCl as minimal reactants to reconstruct flue-gas chemistry. Transition metal species (Cu, Fe) in fly ash catalyze CO conversion via a coupled water–gas shift and Fischer–Tropsch-type process, generating a wide spectrum of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons. Concurrently, fly ash mediates HCl oxidation to active Cl2, enabling chlorination of these intermediates into chlorobenzenes and chlorophenols, which subsequently evolve into polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs), and ultimately PCDD/Fs. Notably, Cl4–8DD/F congeners account for &gt;90% of the formed PCDD/Fs, consistent with de novo synthesis signatures. This work establishes a new mechanistic paradigm for dioxin generation and highlights CO emission control as a critical lever for mitigating toxic pollutant generation.</jats:p>

title:
Advancing Environmental
Justice Research within and
beyond Science and Engineering
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Scientists and engineers have historically approached questions of environmental justice (EJ) differently from social scientists and humanists, from how they formulate problem scope to how they propose solutions. While scientists and engineers have assessed distributional injustices extensively, there are opportunities for deeper interdisciplinary collaboration with other EJ schools of thought. In this Perspective, we first present an EJ schematic for a science and engineering audience, where we trace epistemologies within EJ schools to show how EJ scholars conceptualize knowledge, how this relates to their methods, and how they present and publish work. We survey the EJ literature─mainly work related to the United States─across disciplines to determine major tensions within EJ and between EJ, science, and engineering scholarship. We also discuss possibilities for enabling interdisciplinary collaboration for scientists and engineers working on EJ-related questions by analyzing epistemological compatibilities. Next, we highlight opportunities to facilitate collaboration through an illustrative interdisciplinary case study. We conclude with takeaways for scientists and engineers moving forward, alongside some of the challenges accompanying interdisciplinary EJ research.</jats:p>

title:
Coupling 18F Radiotracer Imaging with Synchrotron
Fe Speciation to Resolve Biogeochemical Dynamics in PHC-Contaminated
Soils

affiliation.name: National Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Laboratory , , ,

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In petroleum hydrocarbon (PHC)-contaminated subsoils, iron bioavailability often is believed to constrain the degradation of PHC contaminants, but spatially resolved evidence linking microbial activity with Fe transformations is scarce. Here, we bridge this gap by integrating phosphor imaging using positron-emitting radiotracer [18F]fluorobenzene─a high-fidelity surrogate for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene (BTEX)─with synchrotron-based X-ray spectroscopy. This multimodal approach allows for targeted mineralogical fingerprinting, guided by direct visualization of microbial activity within PHC-contaminated soils. Bulk X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) showed little contrast, but microspectroscopy analysis revealed diffuse Fe at active zones and discrete Fe grains in inactive matrices, a pattern consistent with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II) and porewater transport before reprecipitation/reoxidation. Zones of high microbial activity were enriched in reactive phases (ferrihydrite, siderite, and green rust) comprising 27–71% of total Fe, whereas inactive matrices sequestered Fe mainly in Ca–Fe silicates with less than 25% reactive Fe. The recurring presence of green rust and vivianite aligns with phosphate-associated early-stage products under long-term tripolyphosphate biostimulation. We conclude that hydrocarbon degradation co-occurs spatially with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II), lateral transport in porewater, and phosphate-associated reoxidation/reprecipitation, processes that bulk methods often obscure but microscale mapping reveals. These insights support potential comanaging Fe and P amendments and targeted delivery of amendments to enhance PHC bioremediation in cold, calcareous soils.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The efficient conversion of CO2 and industrial waste streams into value-added products remains a critical challenge for sustainable microbial processes. Here, we present the first systematic demonstration of purple phototrophic bacteria (PPB) as platforms for the autotrophic valorization of CO2 and industrial off-gases or sulfur byproducts into valuable metabolites. Genome-guided screening combined with experimental validation identified strains capable of coupling photoautotrophic growth with the production of CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments. Among them, Rhodospirillum rubrum DSM 467 and DSM 107 exhibited the highest performance, maintaining stable CO2 and H2 consumption under semicontinuous operation and accumulating up to 9.6 ± 0.2 mgCoQ10 gbiomass–1 under CO2/ H2 conditions, comparable to engineered production systems. In addition, R. rubrum DSM 467 efficiently oxidized CO from syngas via the water–gas shift reaction, displaying hierarchical substrate utilization driven by energetic constraints. In contrast, Marichromatium purpuratum simultaneously oxidized H2 and thiosulfate (S2O32–), enabling parallel electron input into the photosynthetic electron transport chain and enhanced growth. Overall, these results establish PPB as robust and metabolically flexible biocatalysts for converting CO2 and industrial waste streams into high-value chemicals with direct applications in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Atmospheric microplastics (MPs) play an important role in the transport of MPs across diverse environmental media, yet their annual deposition dynamics across heterogeneous urban–cropland regions remain poorly understood. We conducted a one-year field campaign at three contrasting sites in the North China Plain (NCP): Beijing (BJ, urban), Tianjin (TJ, industrial/coastal), and Handan (HD, agricultural). Atmospheric bulk-deposition samples were characterized for particle deposition rates, size, morphology, and polymer composition, with observations evaluated using meteorological and land-cover information. Deposition rates were significantly higher in BJ than in TJ (p &lt; 0.05) and HD (p &lt; 0.001). Median (interquartile range) deposition rates were 34640 (18703–90472), 14367 (6000–25810), and 6990 (3903–11790) items m–2 d–1 in BJ, TJ, and HD, respectively. Small particles (20–50 μm) dominated particle abundance (80.7%), whereas fragments dominated particle morphology (90.4%). Backward trajectories indicated seasonal differences in potential air-mass transport pathways. Integrating particle mass estimates with land-cover data yielded order-of-magnitude estimates of annual atmospheric MP inputs of approximately 6 Gg to urban areas and 17 Gg to cropland in the northern NCP. These results reveal pronounced spatiotemporal variability in atmospheric MP deposition and highlight the dominance of small MP fragments across urban and cropland ecosystems.</jats:p>

Phototropic
Endogenous Heating for Low-Temperature

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biological wastewater treatment in cold regions faces a low-efficiency and high-energy paradox due to low-temperature inhibition. Inspired by plant phototropism, this study reports bioinspired phototropic endogenous heating (Bio-PEH) based on the underwater opto-thermomechanical response. Upon illumination, cryopolymerized macroporous reduced graphene oxide@poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) fibers undergo asymmetric contraction, which reorients the illuminated surface to be normal to the light vector, so as to maximize photothermal flux under oblique incidence. Meanwhile, flash heating further enhances water-confined heat transfer and expands the effective heating domain. Bio-PEH arrays raise bulk wastewater from 7.8 to 30.2 °C, which improves NH4+ removal by 2.8-fold, accounting for 25.3–169.7% enhancement compared with Joule heating (JH), direct solar heating (DH), and static endogenous heating (SEH). Global simulations further indicate multifold thermal compensation at high latitudes with substantial carbon and energy cost reduction. This study provides a biophysically inspired strategy by utilizing opto-thermomechanical response to realize heating of low-temperature wastewater, making wastewater treatment in cold regions more efficient, economical, and sustainable.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tris (1-chloro-2-propyl) phosphate (TCPP) is ubiquitous in estuarine environments. Parental TCPP exposure impaired reproduction and offspring developmental in zebrafish; yet its multigenerational and transgenerational effects and epigenetic mechanisms in estuarine fish remain unknown. Here, Mugilogobius chulae embryos were exposed to TCPP until 25 days posthatching and reared in clean seawater until F2 hatching. Reproductive and gonadal end points were assessed across generations, while gonadal steroidogenesis and whole-body DNA methylation in larvae were analyzed in F0 and F1 to investigate potential endocrine and epigenetic mechanisms. TCPP induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity that was transmitted to F2 embryos, with F1 and F2 lowest observed effect concentrations 1 order of magnitude lower than that in F0. In F0, 100 μg/L TCPP reduced fecundity and male gonadosomatic index. In F1, 10, and 100 μg/L prolonged spawning latency and affected male gonadal development. In F2, 10 μg/L reduced embryonic hatching. Disruption of steroidogenesis gene expression and hormone levels occurred in F0 and F1 male gonads but only in F1 females. Whole-genome DNA methylation revealed persistent hypermethylation of nerve growth factor receptor (NGFR) and calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit γ 2 (CACNG2) in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway across F0 and F1. Their hypermethylation and reduced expression were associated with decreased steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (STAR) and cytochrome P450 family 11 subfamily A member (CYP11A) in male gonads, suggesting NGFR and CACNG2 may represent candidate epigenetically regulated genes associated with TCPP-induced multigenerational reproductive toxicity. This study reveals transgenerational risks of environmental concentrations of TCPP to estuarine fish and provides epigenetic evidence for multigenerational endocrine disruptors.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Activation of lattice oxygen and molecular oxygen critically governs the catalytic degradation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), driving substantial research into harmonizing the bonding state of oxygen atoms in transition-metal oxides to facilitate VOCs abatement. However, the underlying mechanism of oxygen activation via cation substitution in spinel remains to be explored owing to its significant flexibility in both tetrahedral and octahedral sites. Herein, a Mn-substituted FexCo3–xO4 spinel catalyst was developed for promoting oxidation of toluene (one of the typical aromatic VOCs), with the temperature of 90% toluene conversion decreasing by approximately 51 °C relative to the pristine one. Multiple characterizations and theoretical calculations revealed that Mn3+ substitution at octahedral Co3+ sites of FexCo3–xO4 modulated the metal–oxygen bonds within the Mn–O–Co structure for activating surface lattice oxygen, accompanied by the creation of abundant oxygen vacancies for O2 excitation. The combined results of temperature-programmed analyses, isotopic labeling experiments, and in situ spectroscopy showed that the adsorbed toluene could be synchronously oxidized by activated lattice oxygen and chemisorbed oxygen generated via O2 activation, thereby accomplishing the deep oxidation of toluene. This study clarifies the synergistic role of lattice and molecular oxygen in toluene oxidation and affords a potential catalyst for environmental remediation.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Particle size is a key factor influencing metal uptake by aquatic unicellular primary producers. To investigate size-dependent bioconcentration ranging from ions to nanoclusters (NCs) and nanoparticles (NPs), we used cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) to quantitatively examine single-cell uptake, retention, and bioconcentration in Chlorella vulgaris exposed to Au3+ ions, three glutathione (GSH)-protected AuNC preparations (Au10–12SG10–12, Au15SG13, and Au25SG18), and four GSH-coated AuNPs (5, 15, 25, 50 nm). Au3+ and AuNCs showed rapid cell-associated accumulation but followed exponential-decay and two-phase clearance kinetics, indicating efficient cellular elimination and a tendency to be released back into the medium. In contrast, AuNPs followed saturation-type bioconcentration kinetics, with larger particles showing more persistent cell association. Single-cell analysis revealed strong size-dependent heterogeneity: under equal-mass exposure, the fraction of Au-positive cells decreased exponentially with increasing atom number, whereas the Au burden per Au-positive cell increased approximately linearly. Larger particles exhibited higher volume concentration factors (VCFs) with a small subset of “high-VCF” cells. These results highlight that both particle size and cellular heterogeneity jointly govern algal bioconcentration patterns and should be accounted for in environmental risk assessment of metal-based nanomaterials.</jats:p>
